Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test
                 (DAFT)

                30 Day Report





Principal Investigator:
David Urban, NASA Glenn Research Center

Co-Investigators:
George Mulholland, University of Maryland
Zeng-guang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Res earch
Jiann Yang, National Institute for Standards and Technology
Thomas Cleary, National Institute for Standards and Technology



                                       1

Final Research Report Template and Guidelines

I.  Introduction
   A. Abstract

In the wake of the Columbia disaster, NASA Headquarters put out a call for small, low upmass
experiments that could be launched aboard the Russian Progress vehicle and which could be made
a vailable for launch within a six month period from the date of the request (March, 2003).

The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME, formerly known as “Smoke”), which was
being developed at the time and which is designed for operation aboard the ISS, required the
utilization of a commercially available particulate counter, the TSI P-Trak, that is designed to use
gravity to facilitate its operation. The microgravity performance of this instrument was in question
and added significant technical risk to the future success of SAME.

The Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) was designed as a risk mitigation
experiment to test the performance of the P-Trak in a microgravity environment.



    B.  Hypothesis

Two potential failure modes were identified for the device: 1) that the particulate counting system,
containing a nozzle, a laser diode and sensitive optics would clog or become obscured and 2) that
the internal flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device would cause an over counting of the
particulates and give unreliable (high) readings. Therefore, an experiment was designed that would
use a functionally flight like design and test it against an aerosol standar d and another device (the
TSI DustTrak), that was analyzed to be unaffected by the lack of gravity.

The choice of the aerosol and the method used to create it were key items. Ideally, a mono dispersed
aerosol would be used (0.7 – 1.3 microns), which would allow an easy comparison of the readings
from the devices. However, due to the lack of development time, it was proposed to use Arizona
Road Dust (ARD, Fine) instead, in combination with ISS GN2 to create an aerosol for measurement
purposes.

Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses in DAFT: 1) that the TSI P-Trak, as modified for use in
SAME, would function normally in microgravity, and 2) that the aerosol created and  filtered per
the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices

   C. Objectives of Investigation

The  objective  of DAFT was  to minimize  the  risks  of  its  parent  experiment, SAME, by
demonstrating  that  the modified TSI  P-Trak  functioned  effectively  and  predictably  in  a
microgravity environment.


II. Methods/Research Operations

   A. Disc ussion of Method/Protocol

In order to prepare the P-Trak for operation in microgravity, an analysis of its operation was
performed. The P-Trak uses a small pump to draw the sample aerosol through a chamber saturated

                                      2

with alcohol vapor by means of a wick. That vapor/aerosol mix then passes through a cooling tube
that allows the alcohol to condense on the particles in the aerosol, making droplets that are large
enough to count w ith a focused laser/photo cell combination. The condenser in the COTS device
sl opes down, enabling the alcohol from the droplets that adhere to the tube wall to be recycled back
to the evaporator.

In conjunction with fluid physics researchers at GRC, a modification to the cooling tube was
developed that effectively moves liquid alcohol from the tip of the tube back upstream to the
evaporator due to capillary action. This was the major modification that was made to the device.
O ther alterations to the device involved the removal of the mercury switch (for gravitationally
sensitive tilt sensor), flight hardening and covering with foil tape for flammability concerns.

T he TSI DustTrak, a laser scattering device based on Mie scattering and included as a measurement
standard, was hardened in a similar fashion, but did not include a mercury switch.

After some consideration, it was decided to use a 15 liter Mylar bag for the containment of the
aerosol. Issues, including safety and the atomizing of the particulates (and the fluid that con tained
them) precluded the use of commercially a vailable mono-dispersed particles. Therefore, Arizona
R oad Dust (fine), a NIST standard, was selected due to its known constitution and ease of
dispersion into a pressurized gas stream.

A flight design was created, the parameters tested and determined, and flight like hardware was
created and tested with the measurement instruments to develop the correlation curves discussed in
the results section.

One problem exists with this sample material, however.  It contains a given number of particles in
sizes above 2.5 microns, which is above the measurement limit of the P-Trak. To mitigate this
factor, a device, the DAFT Impactor was developed based on design criteria supplied by one of the
e xperiment’s Co-I’s (George Mulholland). The DAFT Impactor is a particle filter for large particles
(only) that was designed specifically for the combined flow rate of the test devices.

The P-Trak gives a number count of the particles in an aerosol, in readings of pt/cc. Dustrak gives
measurements of the total mass, in mg/m3. Since the distribution of the particulates in the a erosol is
known to a certain confidence level, and the units had been correlated in testing on the ground, t he
experiment was conceived to disburse a similar aerosol on orbit and determine the device
corr elation in a microgravity environment to quantify the P-Trak’s measurement effectiveness.

    B.  List & Description of All Functional Objectives

As stated in previous sections, the functional objective of DAFT was to demonstrate the effective
operation of the TSI P-Trak in a microgravity environment. Th is was intended to be accomplished
u tilizing no more than 15 test points of aerosolized ARD in conjunction with a TSI DustTrak to
provide a correlation to the readings obtained from the P-Trak.

Due to th e limitations imposed to the allowable upmass for US based experiments, the DAFT
hardware was d ivided into the following four section s:
DAFT-1       Contained the modified P-Trak, an Alcohol Wick and batt eries
DAFT-2       Contained a DustTrak and batteries
DAFT-3       Contained the s ample generating and filtering equipment
D AFT-4       Contained an unmodified (but flight hardened) P-Trak, another alcohol wick and
             more batteries

Since  all  of  the hardware was  not launched  simultaneously,  the  objectives were modified
accordingly. DAFT-1 and -2 were launched aboard Progress mission 16P, and an opportunity to

                                       3

operate that hardware became available in February of 2005. Since the s ample materials were not
in cluded, the team determined to operate the devices sampling ISS cabin air at various locations. It
was also suggested that particulates could be created by mating and de-mating Velcro in front o f the
sh ared sample port, which was done as described in the Sessions section.

Once DAFT-3 and -4 were brought on orbit, the original experiment objectives were utilized.

   D.  Sessions Table

   D.1    DAFT 1 & 2, Session 1, GMT 54, 2005

   The first test point for DAFT was performed on February 22, 2005 during Increment 10. The
    hardware was set up per the procedure (nominal) in front of EXPRESS Rack 4. Leroy Chiao inserted
    the batteries to each device, activated them, and performed the zero check. No anomalies were noted

                                       4

(i.e.; warnings, beeping, unreasonable readings, blocked tubing, etc.). The P-Trak was operated for
approximately 12 minutes, and continued taking readings for the entire time. Near Real Time (NRT)
video was available for most of the test, including set up, and the run time could be approximately
synchronized with GMT through its use.

The Payload Operations Director (POD) allowed the call up of a request, and Leroy was asked to
relay readings from the P-Trak verbally, which he did. Those readings were low (2 – 5 pt/cc).

The data for that test point can be seen in Section III C. Figures 1 and 2. A review of that data shows
that the readings on both devices were very low for the entire test time, but that upon initial startup,
the addition and removal of the HEPA filter (zero check) is clearly indicated in the P-Trak data, and
there appears to be some residual dust in the sampling tube that is drawn out during the test point. For
the remainder of the point, some small variations can be seen, the DustTrak especially gave low
readings. Overall, these readings are almost an order of magnitude below those that would normally
be seen in a typical laboratory environment ( ~ 4,000 – 6,000 pt/cc for P-Trak), but were not totally
unexpected, due to the presence of a HEPA filter on the ISS air handling system.

D.2  DAFT 1 & 2, Session 2, GMT 63, 2005

On March 4, 2005, DAFT was given its second opportunity, which involved the performance of
three additional test points. The DAFT ground team had made prior arrangements to revise the test
procedure to include alternate techniques and locations in an attempt to realize higher readings on
both of the devices. Leroy was also asked to signal the ground team when he turned on the devices to
allow more precise time synchronization between the devices’ internal clocks and GMT. (Note:
although the units both have internal clocks powered by a coin battery, these clocks drift over time).

Near Real Time (NRT) video was again provided, with a window that extended for approximately 25
minutes; enough to capture all but the last few minutes of test point #4. Leroy gave a ‘thumbs up’
when he turned on each device at the beginning of this session, and through PAYCOM there were
some real time communications regarding the activities during the test points.

For test point #2 Leroy was asked to mate and demate Velcro in front of the intake for the tubing that
supplies samples to both of the devices. That data is provided in Section III C. Figures 3 and 4.Test
points #3 and #4 were taken in Lab 1, adjacent to Port 6 and in the US Node 1, mid-cabin,
respectively.


D.3   DAFT-3, Session 1, GMT 229, 2006

The first test point for DAFT-3 and -4 was scheduled to be performed on August 18, 2006 (GMT
229), during Increment 13. DAFT required NRT Video. During the hardware was set up procedure in
front of EXPRESS Rack 5, Jeff Williams was in the process of unpacking the experiment equipment,
and held each item in front of the camera as he unpacked it. When he held up the DAFT Fill
Assembly, the ground team noticed immediately that the HEPA filter that supports the pressure relief
valves that protect the Sample Bag from being over filled, was missing. The POD was notified and
requested to ask Jeff to return the Fill Assembly into the field of view, which he did, confirming the
observation. Jeff noted that the HEPA Filter Subassembly was still within the foam enclosure. He
then held up that enclosure, and noted that it was permanently deformed. The DAFT Fill Assembly is
a series of linear tubing connections with ‘appendages’ connected to it by tees. The foam that encased
it (minicell) is approximately three times longer than it is wide, and it is about 2 inches thick. From
the video, it was clear that the foam was deformed from flat by about one inch along the shorter axis,
in line with the thickness. The foam is a ‘donut’ like cutout, with no strength in the direction of the
deformation.



                                    5

At that point, the nominal test plan was aborted. Jeff was asked to restow the Fill Assembly, and to
revert to the procedure that was used for DAFT-1 &-2, taking a cabin air sample, which he did. Later,
when he attempted to download the data from the devices, another anomaly occurred. When he had
attached the P-Trak and attempted the data transfer, the message: “Error Communicating” popped up.
The transfer was attempted one more time with the P-Trak and also once with the DustTrak. Backing
up in the procedure and attempting to select a com port revealed that the EXPRESS Laptop being
used did not have a “Com Port 1” within its list of available choices, which was a problem, since the
DAFT Software was configured to use that port.

D.4   DAFT-3, GMT 230, 2006

As a result of the discovery of the broken part on the previous day, a special Safety telecom was
convened to determine if the experiment could be performed, and if so, what level of repair or
modification would be required to provide the necessary protection for the crew. That telecom
involved members of the PSRP, the ISS Cadre, DAFT Project Management and Safety, POIC
Safety, the Crew Office and MER Safety.

The DAFT engineering team provided several options for repair. They are briefly described as
follows:

       Option 1: Cover the opening to the tubing system with a finger tip, or alternately, with gray
         tape, and perform the experiment nominally.

       Option 2: Remove the fitting that supports the Gage subassembly, remove the high pressure
          relief valve from that subassembly and replace it in that location; and use the remaining
          fitting to reinstall the low pressure relief valves, without the HEPA filter.

       Option 3: Disassemble the DAFT Impactor and remove the HEPA filter. Use that HEPA
           filter to replace the broken one on the Fill Assembly and scavenge the parts from the
        Impactor that are necessary to deliver the sample to the devices.

After a significant discussion regarding the implications and ramifications of each potential fix, it was
determined that Option 1, using gray tape to cover the opening, would be the most desirable and did
not pose an undue Safety risk to the crew.

The engineering team worked with the designated Crew Procedures Engineer (Wayne Wright) to
develop the procedures to support that activity, and it was approved for use.

Also, the issue regarding the labeling of the com ports on the ELC was worked with the EXPRESS
Software group. This issue was resolved when the EXPRESS group renamed the ports to be in
compliance with the needs of the DAFT software.

An ISS Payload Anomaly Report (PSR) number (DAFT-HW-01) was issued to describe, record and
document the resolution of the broken DAFT Fill Assembly.

D.5   DAFT-3, Session 1, GMT 233, 2006

Jeff accomplished the repair without incident and proceeded to perform the nominal test procedures.
Since the DAFT ground team realized that this might be the only opportunity to perform the
experiment and in order to insure that the test points would have the maximum experimental value,
POD was asked to direct PAYCOM to ask Jeff to voice down the real-time readings from the P-Trak
and the DustTrak during the sampling period. This would allow the team to know immediately if the
concentration of the aerosol within the Sample Bags was appropriate to keep both of the instruments
within range. It was extremely fortunate that that opportunity was provided to the Science and
Engineering team. Near Real Time Video was also made available whenever there was Ku Band
coverage.

                                    6

The ground team requested that Alcohol Wick S/N 02 be used, to insure that there would be enough
    alcohol to run all of the test points. Jeff was unable to open the container that it was in. The reason for
     that is unknown. He was directed to revert to using Alcohol Wick S/N 01.

   The 2.5 micron Impactor was installed on the DustTrak from the Accessories kit.

     Jeff noted during set up that he could not make the DustTrak go into Log Mode 2. Using voice up
    messaging with POD and PAYCOM, the ground team asked Jeff to make a second attempt, which he
    did, but that did not help. He was instructed to ignore the problem and move forward.

   The number of requested toggles of the fill valve (per the Execution Notes), once the DAFT Dust
    Holder was installed onto the Fill Assembly, was four.

   Both of the instrument’s count values went to zero when the HEPA filter was installed on the DAFT
    Impactor inlet, which is nominal.

   Once the devices were attached, while performing DAFT Sample Extract, Jeff gave a reading from
    each instrument at 30 second intervals for the entire time that sampling was occurring. The data was
    recorded manually by the DAFT ground team. That data has been transcribed to an Excel file and is
    included in Appendix C, labeled as ‘Bag #1’.

   The operations proceeded nominally from this point forward, although the P-Trak reportedly started
    beeping sometime before Bag #2 was extracted. It is unknown if this was an actual low alcohol
    warning, or merely an artifact of drawing the Sample Low enough to cause a vacuum within the P-
    Trak.

   The HEPA filter was installed on the inlet of the DAFT Impactor before each test point and the
    devices were re-zeroed. Six toggles were used to introduce dust into Sample Bag #2. Eight toggles
   were used for Sample Bag #3. Jeff continued to provide call downs of the instrument readings every
   30 seconds for all of the test points, and they were recorded in a similar fashion. The units were not
    turned off in between test points, and no removal or reinstallation of the P-Trak Alcohol Wick was
    performed until the end of the session. All of the used Sample Bags and Dust Holders were placed in
    the trash at the end of the test period. The DAFT hardware was all restowed at the end of the testing,
    since the scheduled Data Download would not be performed for several hours.

   When Jeff attached the P-Trak to the ELC to download the data, it was clear that the fix implemented
   by the EXPRESS team had worked, the device recognized the Com Port, and reported that there
   were four test points ready for downloading. This did not seem to be right, since it was the opinion of
    the ground team that the four test points from the previous testing (last year) should still have been
    stored, and the test numbers should have incremented starting at number 5. The devices were both
    queried for test points 5, 6 and 7, and no data was found. The DATA Download procedure was then
    performed nominally, transferring test points 1 – 4 and those four files were placed on the ELC for
    downlink as a part of their housekeeping data.

    Unfortunately, the only data received electronically once it was transferred from EXPRESS to the
  GRC TSC was the data obtained from the DAFT-1 and -2 over a year ago.


III. Results

   A.  List of Pre-, In-, Postflight Anomalies

    Detailed in the Sessions section.

    B.  Completeness/Quality of Data

                                       7

The data taken from DAFT 1 and 2 can be seen in Section III C. Figures 1 through 4.

Test point #2 data (Figures 3 and 4) shows that the P-Trak responded to the Velcro dust quite well, with
several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark (P-Trak has a maximum count of 500,000 pt/cc). Although
there is no way to exactly correlate between the Velcro demates and the increases in the P-Trak readings,
the observations that the unit’s readings increased and decreased in a logical fashion, were within the
unit’s prescribed range and there were no observed anomalies serve to indicate that the unit was
functioning normally. DustTrak also responded well to the Velcro dust, but did not reach readings above
10% of its overall capability.

Test points #3 and #4 were not appreciably different from Test point #1 for either device.

Section III C. Figure 7 contains a chart developed from the ground testing that was performed in May of
2003, using the crew training hardware in a flight like manner. It can be seen from that graph that
although there is a wide variation in the amount of aerosol that is contained within the various samples,
the relationship between the DustTrak and P-Trak readings is very linear, meaning that the overall
composition of the various aerosols created on the ground, regardless of concentration, is very similar
with regard to the relationship between the number and the sizes of the particles entrained.

A comparison between this chart and the one taken from the flight data, presented in Appendix C, shows
that the data acquired on orbit falls outside of this ground based relationship. The data points are clustered
to the left of the line (area), in a region where the count/mass ratio is lower than what was determined
from ground testing. This indicates then, that the mass of the average particle counted on orbit is higher
than that determined on Earth. This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive
settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained.

It should be noted that, although the DAFT Impactor is designed to filter out the larger particles, it is only
about 50% efficient; which implies that it is allowing a considerable number of larger particles to be
drawn into the devices.

If the data collected on orbit had been to the lower right of the ground based testing line on the graph in
Appendix D, it would have meant that more smaller particles would have been present; which is counter
intuitive and would have indicated that the P-Trak may have been over counting the particles, one of the
postulated failure modes.

The analysis of the average particulate size and mass shown on the spreadsheet in Figure 5 (provided by
Zengguang Yuan) shows a good uniformity between the particulates sampled from the various bags. The
average mass (assuming a material density of water) is 2.5 E-12 grams, with a range from 2 – 3 E-12. The
calculated average diameter is 1.65 micron, ranging from 1.56 – 1.7 micron.

The sample material, Arizona Road Dust (Fine) is a standardized, homogenous material; but since it
contains a wide distribution of sizes, it is a mixture. The amount of the material that is enclosed in each
Dust Holder is small (0.25 gram). From ground testing, it is estimated that only about 10% of the material
contained within the Dust Holder is introduced into the aerosol, due to the irregular interior surfaces
within it, the surface adhesion of the dust and other factors. Therefore, the net amount of sample delivered
to the Sample Bags is about 25 milligrams. Since this amount is so small and is coming from a mixture,
some variation in the average particle size between samples is expected.

H. Conclusion


Ideally, DAFT would have collected electronic data from all of the planned 15 test points to establish a
large body of consistent, repeated data. Several factors contributed to the decision to not pursue additional
test points. They were:

Crew Time: Although DAFT was planned for Increment 13, there was not enough crew time available to
support all of the desired Payload activities and the prospects for actually performing the experiment at all
were extremely uncertain. Fortunately for DAFT, ALTEA had some problems with their hardware and a
small block of time came open. DAFT had to negotiate very hard to be allowed the opportunity to
schedule 1 + 3 test points, and there was very little chance for another session.

Isopropyl Alcohol: As mentioned in the Results section, Jeff Williams was unable to open the DAFT
Alcohol Wick container -02. This limited the amount of alcohol available to support the operation of the
P-Trak. Leroy Chiao used this alcohol wick when he performed DAFT-1 and -2 and both of those units
were loaded with alcohol over 3 years ago, so the amount that is remaining is highly questionable.

Sample Build Up: Testing in the lab has shown that under some circumstances, especially when a
significant amount of the larger ARD particles is sent to the devices, a buildup of particles can occur
within the optics chamber of the P-Trak. Clearly, the data shows that the sample aerosol contained a
greater proportion of larger particles than is experienced on Earth. It also shows that as the run time on the
P-Trak is increasing, especially during Bag #3, the count/mass ratio is declining. Although it is not certain
that this build up is occurring, the symptoms of that condition are consistent with the data.

The lack of the electronic data collection has limited the ability of the project team to perform a more
detailed analysis of the data, since it will remain unknown as to the actual range of the readings over time.
The team feels that the information gathered and transmitted by Jeff does represent a good average, but
details regarding the data spread could well be lost and not retrievable, since the log functions on both
machines seem to have failed (although the possibility of operator error does remain).

Based on the limited availability of the crew, it does not seem reasonable to think that time and
procedures could be made available for Jeff or the follow on Increment 14 crew to troubleshoot the
devices.

That being said, DAFT was conceived and built as a Risk Mitigation experiment, not necessarily a
Science experiment. It was delivered only 6 months after being proposed and accepted, and it was
understood that in some respects, the sample material (the ARD, a poly disperse particulate) was less than
ideal.

(Note: For those unfamiliar with the experiment, ideally, a mono disperse aerosol with particulates about
0.7 microns in size would have been created in a density of about 50,000 pt/cc in order to provide a more
quantifiable relationship between the readings from the DustTrak and P-Trak. Unfortunately, an aerosol
of this type is difficult to manufacture, and the project did not have time or resources to attempt such a
development.)

The data shows that the devices were able to operate in microgravity for an extended period of time with
no apparent failure. One of the major concerns was that the P-Trak would accumulate alcohol in the
optics chamber and obscure them, causing the unit to either read ‘0’ or display and error code. This did
not happen. The units gave readings from zero well up into the middle of their operational ranges, and
then back; in short, they performed as expected.

DAFT-1 and -2 showed that the units were ‘apparently working’ and that the air aboard the ISS is almost
unbelievably clean. The readings from the devices during that part of the overall experiment though,
never crossed the 20% of the operational range threshold, leaving the results somewhat suspect.


                                      13

This latest experimental run, however, did. The project team feels that the optimal reading range for the
P-Trak is from 30,000 – 100,000 pt/cc (although the published range goes up to 500,000 pt/cc) and for
the DustTrak; 20 – 80 mg/m3. Clearly, the latest data was within this range.

The count/mass ratio between the devices as measured on orbit, although well outside of the value
determined on Earth, is both explainable and credible; and to the best of the team’s ability to analyze the
data, seems very consistent.

The problems with the equipment and the data have been discussed at some length, and although they do
leave something to be desired, it does appear that there is enough consistency to determine that the
readings recorded are believable and representative of the aerosol created, implying that the units both
functioned nominally.

Due to the constraints listed above, DAFT-4, using the ‘unmodified’ P-Trak, was not performed. Since
the flight hardware for SAME has been manufactured to the same specifications as the unit that was
tested (P-Trak-01), this is not considered to be a factor.

The Science team has examined the data and compared the results against the empirical data accumulated
for polydisperse aerosols; and determined that the results do have a good basis for acceptance within the
bounds of that analysis.

For these reasons, the SAME (DAFT) project team feels that the DAFT experiment has been a complete
success, and that it has confidence that the P-Traks as designed and manufactured for SAME will perform
as accurately and effectively on-orbit as they have in the labs.

      I.     Earth Benefits / Spin-off Applications

       There are no tangible Earth benefits from this experiment.





                                      14
